title: Employee turnover in supermarkets: statistical consulting for an undergraduate thesis
text:
The request
A Business Administration student was finishing an undergraduate thesis titled Leadership, recognition and turnover intention among supermarket employees in central-western Minas Gerais. He ran a Google Forms survey in stores across the region: profile questions plus 20 statements rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), in five blocks.









Block
Items
Sample statement




Leadership
5
“My supervisor treats me with respect.”


Recognition
4
“I get praise for my work.”


Perceived pay
4
“My pay is fair for the work I do.”


Work-life balance
4
“I can plan my days off in advance.”


Turnover intention
3
“I plan to look for another job in the next 12 months.”




The project had four hypotheses:

H1. Better-rated leadership reduces the intention to leave.
H2. More recognition reduces the intention to leave.
H3. Better-rated pay reduces the intention to leave, with a smaller effect than H1 and H2.
H4. Better work-life balance reduces the intention to leave.

He had the spreadsheet exported from Forms and his advisor’s instruction to “do the statistics part.” He needed to know what to run, in what order, how to check whether he could trust the results and how to report everything in the thesis.

title: Employee turnover in supermarkets: statistical consulting for an undergraduate thesis
text:
What I did

1. Cleaning


Show the R code
bruto <- read_csv("dados/respostas_brutas.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dic <- read_csv("dados/dicionario.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# O Forms exporta o texto inteiro da pergunta como nome da coluna;
# o dicionário troca cada um por um código curto (LID1, REC2...).
names(bruto) <- dic$codigo[match(names(bruto), dic$coluna)]
itens <- filter(dic, construto != "Perfil") |>
  mutate(enunciado = str_match(coluna, "\\[(.*)\\]$")[, 2])
cod <- itens$codigo
blocos <- split(cod, substr(cod, 1, 3))

brancos <- function(df) rowSums(is.na(select(df, all_of(cod))))
iguais <- function(df) apply(select(df, all_of(cod)), 1, sd, na.rm = TRUE) == 0

passo1 <- filter(bruto, aceite == "Sim")
passo2 <- filter(passo1, brancos(passo1) <= 4)      # até 20% dos 20 itens em branco
passo3 <- filter(passo2, !iguais(passo2))           # mesma resposta nos 20 itens

excluidas <- c(sem_aceite = nrow(bruto) - nrow(passo1), brancos = nrow(passo1) - nrow(passo2),
               iguais = nrow(passo2) - nrow(passo3))
celulas_brancas <- sum(is.na(select(passo3, all_of(cod))))


Of the 230 responses received, 212 went on to the analysis. Each exclusion has a reason that can be written into the thesis methods section:

Someone who gives the same answer to everything, including the reversed leadership item (“My supervisor rarely gives me feedback”), is saying at the same time that the supervisor does and does not give feedback: a sign they did not read the statements.
The valid responses still had 87 scattered blank items (2.1% of cells). The rule was simple and is written into the report: each block’s score is the mean of the items answered, as long as no more than 1 item in the block is blank. Two people left 2 Work-life balance items blank and have no score for that block.
Age group was a free-text field, and everyone wrote it their own way. A text rule merged the variants (the middle column shows the original data, in Portuguese):

padronizar_faixa <- function(x) {

3. Scale reliability
Before adding statements up into a score, you have to show that they measure the same thing. I used two indicators: Cronbach’s alpha, which the advisor and the thesis committee expect to see, and McDonald’s omega, which is better suited when the statements do not all carry the same weight in the construct. Above .70 is the usual threshold.


Show the R code
confiab <- function(cols) {
  x <- select(d, all_of(cols))
  c(alfa = suppressWarnings(psych::alpha(x)$total$raw_alpha),
    omega = suppressMessages(suppressWarnings(psych::omega(x, nfactors = 1, plot = FALSE)$omega.tot)))
}
rem_sem4 <- c("REM1", "REM2", "REM3")
conf <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(blocos), function(b) c(bloco = b, itens = length(blocos[[b]]), confiab(blocos[[b]]))),
  c(bloco = "REM_sem4", itens = 3, confiab(rem_sem4))
) |>
  mutate(across(c(itens, alfa, omega), as.numeric)) |>
  arrange(match(bloco, c("LID", "REC", "REM", "REM_sem4", "EQU", "INT")))

# Correlação de cada item de Remuneração com o total dos outros três.
r_rem <- psych::alpha(select(d, all_of(blocos$REM)))$item.stats$r.drop
names(r_rem) <- blocos$REM

Four blocks passed comfortably. Perceived pay came in at .68 because of one item: “I receive my transportation allowance on time” (REM4) barely moves with the other three (a correlation of .09 with their total, against .58 or more for the rest). That makes sense: it measures whether a benefit arrives on time, not whether the pay feels fair. Without it, alpha rises to .82. REM4 was dropped from the Perceived pay score, and the thesis records that decision and the reason for it.


4. Exploratory factor analysis
Factor analysis checks whether the 20 statements group into the five blocks the questionnaire intended. Because the answers are ordinal (1 to 5), I used polychoric correlation, which treats each answer as a band on an underlying continuous scale and does not assume that the distance between “1” and “2” equals the distance between “4” and “5”.


Show the R code
x_itens <- select(d, all_of(cod))
pc <- suppressWarnings(polychoric(x_itens)$rho)
kmo <- KMO(pc)$MSA
bartlett <- cortest.bartlett(pc, n = nrow(d))
fe <- suppressWarnings(fa(x_itens, nfactors = 5, cor = "poly", rotate = "oblimin", fm = "minres"))

cargas <- unclass(fe$loadings)
# Dá a cada fator o código do bloco cujos itens carregam mais nele.
dominante <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(cargas)), function(f) {
  names(which.max(tapply(abs(cargas[, f]), substr(rownames(cargas), 1, 3), mean)))
})
colnames(cargas) <- dominante
cargas <- cargas[, c("LID", "REC", "REM", "EQU", "INT")]
carga_rem4 <- max(abs(cargas["REM4", ]))


The KMO was .84 (above .80 is considered very good) and Bartlett’s test gave χ²(190) = 2,198.0, p < .001: the correlations between the statements are strong enough for factor analysis. With five factors and an oblique rotation (the constructs are allowed to correlate), each statement loaded on its own block, with one exception we already knew about: REM4 did not load on any factor (highest loading 0.14), which confirms the reliability decision.

escore <- function(cols) {
  m <- as.matrix(select(d, all_of(cols)))
  if_else(rowSums(is.na(m)) <= 1, rowMeans(m, na.rm = TRUE), NA_real_)
}
d <- d |>
  mutate(LID = escore(blocos$LID), REC = escore(blocos$REC), REM = escore(rem_sem4),
         EQU = escore(blocos$EQU), INT = escore(blocos$INT))


Likert scale scores tend to be skewed and full of ties, so I compared the intention to leave across groups with non-parametric tests, always reporting the effect size, which tells you whether a difference is large or merely statistically detectable.

mw <- wilcox_test(d, INT ~ turno_grupo)
mw_r <- wilcox_effsize(d, INT ~ turno_grupo)
kw <- kruskal_test(d, INT ~ tempo_casa)
kw_e <- kruskal_effsize(d, INT ~ tempo_casa)
dunn <- dunn_test(d, INT ~ tempo_casa, p.adjust.method = "holm")
dunn_novato <- filter(dunn, group1 == "Até 1 ano", p.adj < 0.05)

resumo_grupos <- function(var) {

    summarise(n = n(), mediana = median(INT), q1 = quantile(INT, .25), q3 = quantile(INT, .75))
}
grupos <- bind_rows(resumo_grupos("turno_grupo"), resumo_grupos("tempo_casa"))

7. Multiple regression
Correlation looks at one factor at a time. To test the hypotheses, the question is different: how much does each factor matter when the others are in the same model? I used multiple linear regression with the four scores standardized (so the effects are comparable) and three controls: night shift, up to 1 year of tenure and sex.


Show the R code
dm <- d |>
  transmute(INT = INT, LID = LID, REC = REC, REM = REM, EQU = EQU,
            noturno = as.numeric(turno == "Noite"),
            novato = as.numeric(tempo_casa == "Até 1 ano"),
            feminino = as.numeric(sexo == "Feminino")) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(across(c(INT, LID, REC, REM, EQU), \(v) as.numeric(scale(v))))
modelo <- lm(INT ~ LID + REC + REM + EQU + noturno + novato + feminino, data = dm)

# Pressupostos
vifs <- vif(modelo)
bp <- bptest(modelo)
sw <- shapiro.test(residuals(modelo))
cook_max <- max(cooks.distance(modelo))

# Erros-padrão robustos (HC3): protegem os testes se a variância dos resíduos não for constante.
v_hc3 <- vcovHC(modelo, type = "HC3")
rob <- coeftest(modelo, vcov. = v_hc3)
ic <- coefci(modelo, vcov. = v_hc3)
resultado <- tibble(termo = rownames(rob), beta = rob[, 1], ep = rob[, 2], p = rob[, 4],
                    li = ic[, 1], ls = ic[, 2]) |>
  filter(termo != "(Intercept)")
ajuste <- summary(modelo)
# H3 diz que o efeito da remuneração é menor: testa se os coeficientes são iguais.
igual_lid <- linearHypothesis(modelo, "REM = LID", vcov. = v_hc3)
igual_rec <- linearHypothesis(modelo, "REM = REC", vcov. = v_hc3)
teste <- function(h) c(F = h$F[2], gl1 = h$Df[2], gl2 = h$Res.Df[2], p = h$`Pr(>F)`[2])
menor_confirmado <- igual_lid$`Pr(>F)`[2] < 0.05 && igual_rec$`Pr(>F)`[2] < 0.05
# O texto das páginas foi escrito para o caso em que a diferença não se confirma.
stopifnot(!menor_confirmado)

# H3 tem duas partes: reduz (testada pelo β) e com efeito menor (testada acima).
hipoteses <- tibble(termo = c("LID", "REC", "REM", "EQU")) |>
  left_join(resultado, by = "termo") |>
  mutate(decisao = case_when(!(beta < 0 & p < 0.05) ~ "nao",
                             termo == "REM" & !menor_confirmado ~ "parcial",
                             TRUE ~ "sim"))


Before reading the coefficients, I checked the assumptions:

Multicollinearity: highest VIF of 1.47, well below the usual limit of 5. The blocks are correlated, but not to the point of being confounded.
Residual variance: Breusch-Pagan test, p = .713. No strong sign of non-constant variance; even so, the tests use robust standard errors (HC3), which cost little and protect the result.
Normality of residuals: Shapiro-Wilk, p = .049. With more than 200 cases, a slight departure does not compromise the coefficient tests.
Influential cases: highest Cook’s distance of 0.04, far below 1. No single response changes the result.

The model explains 43% of the variation in the intention to leave (adjusted R² = .41, N = 210).
H3 says the effect of pay is smaller than those of leadership and recognition. Looking at the βs is not enough: you have to test whether the difference between them is real. The test of equality of coefficients (with the same HC3 correction) did not confirm the difference: F(1, 202) = 3.02, p = .084 against leadership and F(1, 202) = 1.92, p = .167 against recognition.

title: Employee turnover in supermarkets: statistical consulting for an undergraduate thesis
text:
What the data showed


Show the R code
grafico_likert <- function(res, tx) {
  enunciados <- if (is.null(tx$enunciados)) setNames(res$itens$enunciado, res$itens$codigo) else tx$enunciados
  cod <- res$itens$codigo
  inv <- if_else(res$itens$invertido == "sim", paste0(" (", tx$invertido, ")"), "")
  rotulos_itens <- setNames(paste0(cod, inv, ": ", enunciados[cod]), cod)
  cores_likert <- setNames(c("#6a4fa3", "#b9aee0", "#d9dbe1", "#9dbde8", cor[["azul"]]), tx$likert)

  # Barras divergentes: a resposta neutra fica metade de cada lado do zero.
  lik <- res$respostas |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "codigo", values_to = "resposta") |>
    drop_na() |>
    count(codigo, resposta) |>
    group_by(codigo) |>
    complete(resposta = 1:5, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
    arrange(resposta, .by_group = TRUE) |>
    mutate(p = n / sum(n),
           inicio = -(p[1] + p[2] + p[3] / 2) + lag(cumsum(p), default = 0),
           fim = inicio + p, meio = (inicio + fim) / 2) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(nivel = factor(tx$likert[resposta], tx$likert),
           bloco = factor(tx$blocos[substr(codigo, 1, 3)], tx$blocos),
           item = factor(rotulos_itens[codigo], rev(rotulos_itens)))
  totais <- lik |>
    group_by(item, bloco) |>
    summarise(discorda = sum(p[resposta <= 2]), concorda = sum(p[resposta >= 4]), .groups = "drop")
  rotulados <- filter(lik, p >= 0.12)

  ggplot(lik, aes(y = item)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = inicio, xend = fim, yend = item, colour = nivel), linewidth = 7) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_text(data = rotulados, aes(x = meio, label = tx$pct(p)), size = 3, family = "Montserrat",
              colour = if_else(rotulados$resposta %in% c(1, 5), "white", cor[["profundo"]])) +
    geom_text(data = totais, aes(x = -0.82, label = tx$pct(discorda)), hjust = 1, size = 2.8,
              family = "Montserrat", colour = cor[["cinza"]]) +
    geom_text(data = totais, aes(x = 0.82, label = tx$pct(concorda)), hjust = 0, size = 2.8,
              family = "Montserrat", colour = cor[["cinza"]]) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(bloco), scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", labeller = label_wrap_gen(14)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = cores_likert, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.92, 0.92), breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), labels = \(x) tx$pct(abs(x))) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = label_wrap_gen(40)) +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE, override.aes = list(linewidth = 4))) +

title: Absenteeism Radar
text:
The problem
A logistics operator with four distribution centers and about 1,250 people tracked absenteeism with a single monthly number. Over two years it did not move: 3.77% in 2024 and 3.77% in 2025. As far as leadership was concerned, the issue was under control.
Operations managers disagreed. They talked about more overtime to cover night-shift absences and more accidents among new hires. The number was right, and so was the perception; what was missing was a way to see both at once.

title: Absenteeism Radar
text:
What the dashboard showed

The stability was arithmetic. The end of an infectious disease outbreak and fewer long-term absences offset an 8% rise in all other short-term absences.
The rise had an address. In two night-shift teams at the Duque de Caxias site, one in Picking and one in Shipping (Separação e Expedição), the short-term rate went from 3.5% to 6.5% starting in April 2025. The rest of that site and the night shift at the other sites did not change. Both teams had changed supervisors a few weeks earlier: a lead worth investigating, not a conclusion.
The night shift has a higher rate across the whole company (adjusted rate ratio of 1.31), and new hires are absent 1.8 times as often.
A few events account for many hours: 1.6% of events make up 34% of lost hours.
One apparent association was spurious. Large teams seemed to have more absences, but the only very large team worked nights. Once you split by shift, the effect disappears.

title: Absenteeism Radar
text:
How it was built
The data. Thirteen tables in the export format of a Brazilian ERP: pseudonymized records for 1,826 people, scheduled hours for every day (662 thousand rows) and 13.6 thousand absence events. Recording each day’s scheduled hours is what makes it possible to calculate the rate in hours and handle late arrivals, part-time schedules, vacations and mid-month hires correctly. I also injected 146 typical extraction defects (duplicates, reversed dates, orphan keys, inconsistent spellings) so the data cleaning had something concrete to solve.
The cleaning. 26 Power Query queries clean and validate the data. One dashboard page shows what was fixed and how much, so readers know whether they can trust the numbers.
The model. A star schema with three fact tables at different grains (scheduled hours, absence per day and absence event) and 97 DAX measures, organized by topic.
The statistics. Three choices define the project:

Break it down before comparing. The total rate is always split into short-term (up to 15 days, the part a line manager can influence) and long-term (absences managed by occupational health).
Require evidence before raising an alarm. An area is flagged as critical only if the deviation is large and statistically consistent (z-score of event frequency). A six-person team with one long absence does not trigger an alert.
Test the obvious associations. A negative binomial model, adjusted for site, department, shift, age, sex, tenure and year, separated what holds up (night shift, tenure, site) from what does not (team size, sex).

The report as code. A single specification describes every visual (position, fields, measures and the question it answers). From it, a Python script generated the first version of the report, in Power BI’s project format, along with the documentation and the wireframes. The dashboard was then refined in Power BI Desktop. An audit script still checks that every measure used exists in the model and that every number quoted matches the data.
Privacy as a requirement. No names, national ID numbers or email addresses; health reasons only in aggregate; groups smaller than 10 people suppressed; row-level security by site and by manager; and an explicit note that the dashboard is not meant for disciplinary use.

title: Absenteeism Radar

What this project demonstrates

Understanding the business before opening Power BI: the right question was “where did the rate get worse”, not “what is the rate”.
Dimensional modeling and DAX on data with different grains and calculation rules that change the result.
Statistics applied to decisions: decomposition, consistency tests and control for confounding, without mistaking association for cause.
Design and communication: each page answers one question, status is always labeled and the palette is restrained.
Governance and privacy: documented rules, visible data quality and protection for small groups.

title: One number, three answers: KPI governance at Vallora Logística
text:
The story
At the July 2025 results meeting, Vallora heard three absenteeism rates for June. HR showed 4.38%, Operations 3.54% and Finance 2.15%, and the meeting spent half an hour arguing about which one was right.










Absenteeism rate calculated each department’s way, from January 2024 to December 2025. The vertical line marks June 2025, the month discussed at the July meeting.















Absenteeism rate calculated each department’s way, from January 2024 to December 2025. The vertical line marks June 2025, the month discussed at the July meeting.





None of them was wrong. Each department calculated what it needed for its own work and gave the result the same name. The problem was not arithmetic, it was governance: nobody had written down what “absenteeism rate” meant at the company, or who got to decide.
The scene repeated itself over the following months, and in December leadership asked for an inventory of every KPI that circulated in the monthly presentations. Forty turned up, from six departments, and only 13 were well defined. The work took five weeks, in four stages:

Interviews with the people who produce the numbers and the people who use them, in all six departments.
Inventory and diagnosis of each KPI.
Definition sheets for the KPIs that go to leadership.
Governance rules: who proposes, who approves, how a change is recorded.

title: One number, three answers: KPI governance at Vallora Logística
section: The divergence: three calculations, one name
text:
The divergence: three calculations, one name
The three rates come from the same data and answer different questions. The decision was to keep all three, each with its own name, and reserve “Absenteeism rate” for HR’s definition, which is the same as the Radar’s.

HROperationsFinanceQuestion it answersHow much of the contracted time was lost?How many scheduled shifts went uncovered?How much do we pay for hours not worked?NumeratorAbsence hours of every type, including long-term absencesScheduled days with any absence, including late arrivals or early departures of more than 10 minutesAbsence hours paid by the company: doctor's notes, the first 15 days of sick or injury leave, and statutory leaveDenominatorScheduled working hoursScheduled days (people absent for more than 15 days come off the schedule)Scheduled working hoursUnitHoursDaysHours2024 value3.77%3.55%2.19%2025 value3.77%3.48%2.12%Name after the projectAbsenteeism rate (official, goes to leadership)Schedule absence rate (managed by Operations)Cost of paid hours not worked (managed by Finance)HRQuestion it answersHow much of the contracted time was lost?NumeratorAbsence hours of every type, including long-term absencesDenominatorScheduled working hoursUnitHours2024 value3.77%2025 value3.77%Name after the projectAbsenteeism rate (official, goes to leadership)OperationsQuestion it answersHow many scheduled shifts went uncovered?NumeratorScheduled days with any absence, including late arrivals or early departures of more than 10 minutesDenominatorScheduled days (people absent for more than 15 days come off the schedule)UnitDays2024 value3.55%2025 value3.48%Name after the projectSchedule absence rate (managed by Operations)FinanceQuestion it answersHow much do we pay for hours not worked?NumeratorAbsence hours paid by the company: doctor's notes, the first 15 days of sick or injury leave, and statutory leaveDenominatorScheduled working hoursUnitHours2024 value2.19%2025 value2.12%Name after the projectCost of paid hours not worked (managed by Finance)


Operations. Operations counts the whole day even when the absence is a late arrival, which pushes the rate up, but takes anyone absent for more than 15 days off the schedule, which pulls it down. On balance, it lands a little below HR. In four of the 24 months (January and February 2024, September and November 2025), the balance flipped: in months with few long-term absences, counting the whole day weighs more, and Operations comes out above HR.
Finance. It leaves out unexcused absences and late arrivals that are docked from pay, and whatever INSS pays from day 16 of a leave. That is why it runs well below the other two. In Brazil, the employer pays the first 15 days of sick or injury leave; from day 16 on, the social security agency (INSS) pays.



Show the R code for the three definitions
# Tipos da base: 1 atestado médico, 2 consulta ou exame (parcial), 3 acidente
# de trabalho, 4 afastamento do INSS, 5 falta injustificada, 6 atraso ou saída
# antecipada, 7 licença legal (CLT art. 473), 8 acompanhamento de dependente,
# 9 licença maternidade/paternidade (dias já fora da jornada no Radar).
# RH: horas de ausência dos tipos que contam no Radar ÷ horas previstas.
rh <- ausencias |> filter(considera_taxa == 1)

# Operação: dias escalados com qualquer ausência (atraso ou saída antecipada só
# acima de 10 minutos) ÷ dias escalados. Quem está afastado há mais de 15 dias
# (do 16º dia de um evento longo em diante) sai da escala, no numerador e no
# denominador.
afastado <- ausencias |> filter(dias_corridos > 15, dia_do_evento > 15) |> distinct(id_funcionario, data)
escala <- jornada |> anti_join(afastado, c("id_funcionario", "data"))
dias_com_ausencia <- escala |>
  semi_join(filter(ausencias, id_tipo_ausencia != 6 | horas_ausencia * 60 > 10), c("id_funcionario", "data"))

# Financeiro: horas pagas pela empresa ÷ horas previstas. Entram atestados e
# acidentes de até 15 dias, consultas, licenças legais e os 15 primeiros dias
# dos afastamentos longos por doença ou acidente (tipos 1, 3 e 4), que a empresa
# paga por lei. Ficam fora faltas e atrasos (descontados), o que o INSS paga e
# o acompanhamento de dependente.
pagas <- ausencias |>
  filter(id_tipo_ausencia == 7 |
           (id_tipo_ausencia %in% c(1, 2, 3) & dias_corridos <= 15) |
           (id_tipo_ausencia %in% c(1, 3, 4) & dias_corridos > 15 & dia_do_evento <= 15))

The monthly meeting traded six presentations and 40 numbers for a single page with 14 KPIs, each with its owner in the room to explain it. title: One number, three answers: KPI governance at Vallora Logística
text:
What this case demonstrates

Separating the math from the governance. A divergence is rarely a calculation error; it is almost always the lack of a written definition and of someone who decides.
Cutting without deleting. Twenty-six KPIs left the leadership meeting, and no department lost information it needs.
Definition sheets that answer the questions that start arguments: what goes in, what stays out, whether higher is better, when the number closes.
Changes on record, so that today’s number stays comparable with last year’s.
A bridge to BI. The definition sheets become the DAX measures and the dashboard’s data dictionary, and the dashboard stops hiding rules.
